title: “East of Eden” Is at the Library; Now It Comes to TV
content:
Florence Pugh and Zoe Kazan, the star and screenwriter (respectively) of Netflix’s “East of Eden,” a fresh take on John Steinbeck’s classic 1952 California novel, recently came to the Library to get a look at some original Steinbeck material.

Among other items on display, there were signed first editions of “Eden,” manuscript pages from “The Grapes of Wrath” and a dozen or so books from the 19th and early 20th centuries that documented the land and the people of the Salinas Valley, the primary setting of “Eden,” “Of Mice and Men” and other Steinbeck works.

The seven-episode series, which debuts tomorrow,  will stretch, like the book, from the end of the Civil War to World War I. It will also be a tale of good and evil, like the book, but is more centered around the lightning rod character of Cathy Ames, played by Pugh.

“I believe there are monsters born in the world to human parents,” Steinbeck writes in introducing Cathy in the novel, a famous sentence that also begins the series’ trailer, already viewed more than 5 million times on YouTube alone.

title: Superman, Captain America, Kermit the Frog and The Declaration of Independence
content:
This is a guest post by Nyla Adams, a recent intern in the Office of Communications.

The Declaration of Independence didn’t just make American pop culture possible — often, it’s been the star of the show.

In “National Treasure,” the 2004 popcorn thriller, Nicolas Cage must somehow steal the Declaration from the National Archives (it has a secret map on the back) to keep it from getting … really stolen. It’s complicated.

Or in “Hamilton,” Lin-Manuel Miranda’s Pulitzer Prize-winning 2015 musical (still on Broadway!), Angelica Schuyler and Thomas Jefferson each rap famous lines from Jefferson’s work on the Declaration.

In the Bicentennial mania of 1976, comic-book readers watched both Superman and Captain American travel back in time to save the Declaration’s origin story.

And on television and cable, the Declaration has popped up (mostly being quoted) in everything from “Star Trek” to “The Andy Griffith Show” to the HBO miniseries “John Adams” to … you get the idea.

title: How the Poet Mary Oliver was “Saved by the Beauty of the World”
content:
Filmmaker Sasha Waters wasn’t shy when asked at the National Book Festival about the legacy of her latest documentary subject, the poet Mary Oliver: “I think we’re going to think of her as the (Walt) Whitman of the 20th century.”

That’s an almost impossible standard, as Whitman became synonymous with the American spirit in the late 19th century with poems such as “I Hear America Singing,” “Song of Myself,” “O Captain! My Captain!” and “I Sing the Body Electric.” He has since become an iconic American personality of the age, along with the likes of Abraham Lincoln, Mark Twain and Frederick Douglass.

But Oliver, who adored Whitman’s work, won the Pulitzer Prize and the National Book Award for her rapturous odes to nature and our connection to it. She was adored about as much as any poet since Whitman when she died, at 83, in 2019.

title: Carl Sandburg, Woody Guthrie, Pete Seeger, Lead Belly & One Legendary Banjo
content:
—This article also appears in the September/October issue of the Library of Congress Magazine.

It was 1939, and friends gathered in the bohemian heart of Greenwich Village to toast the publication of a new book by one of their own. Frank Warner, a musician and folksong collector, arrived with a prized new possession in hand: a handmade banjo, fresh from the mountains of North Carolina.

Nathan Hicks had crafted this fretless, five-string instrument from figured walnut just months earlier, and Warner quickly customized it to his own style, adding frets and removing the drone string.

That evening, amid the good cheer and easy laughter, Warner impulsively decided on another alteration. He turned to Carl Sandburg, the famed poet, song collector and Lincoln biographer, and held out the banjo. Would you mind signing it?

Sandburg obliged, scrawling his name and the year beneath the bottom string.

The banjo Nathan Hicks crafted in 1939, now with 260 signatures. American Folklife Center. Photo: Shawn Miller.

That, as it turned out, was just the start.
snippet: —This article also appears in the September/October issue of the Library of Congress Magazine.
creator: Mark Hartsell
sourceDescription: Stories from the Library of Congress

title: The American Folklife Center Turns 50: See the New Exhibit
content:
—This is a guest post by Stephen Winik, a folklorist in the American Folklife Center. It also appears in the September/October issue of the Library of Congress Magazine.

The American Folklife Center turns 50 in 2026, marking a half century of preserving, presenting and supporting folk culture. The celebration culminates in mid-September with the opening of a major exhibition, “Alive in Many Hands: The American Folklife Center at 50.”

The center owes its existence to the American Folklife Preservation Act of 1976. Congress charged it with safeguarding the nation’s living cultural traditions — everything from fiddle tunes and quilt patterns to holiday rituals, occupational skills and family recipes. These expressions belong to families, ethnic communities, work groups, religious congregations and regions, stretching from the mainland to the Caribbean and Pacific Islands.

Today, the center maintains one of the largest folklife archives anywhere. It exchanges knowledge and expertise with scholars and communities and produces public programs that bring these traditions to life.

title: A “High Octane” Kate McKinnon at the National Book Festival
content:
-This is a guest post by Sahar Kazmi, a public affairs specialist in the Office of the Chief Information Officer.

“I’m so shy!” Kate McKinnon belted out just moments after dancing across the ballroom stage at the National Book Festival, delighting the huge crowd that turned out for her appearance on the Main Stage.

In conversation with broadcast journalist Amna Nawaz, McKinnon — a New York Times bestselling author and Emmy-winning comedian who starred on Saturday Night Live for a decade — said that even though she loves people and performance, she is actually “the most introvert you could possibly be.”

Her jovial, joke-filled interview, along with a Q&A that saw McKinnon bounding from one end of the stage to the other (and even hopping into the crowd to get a closer listen to one attendee’s question), offered no doubt that the author can turn on her social battery when she needs to. McKinnon was at this year’s festival to discuss her popular middle-grade book series about the eccentric scientist Millicent Quibb and her three young protégés, the Porch sisters.


(The full video of McKinnon’s appearance at the National Book Festival is at the link above. Her segment begins at 1:52:00.)

title: Helping Homeless Kids with Reading: Brazil’s Projeto Uerê Wins Library’s Top Literacy Award
content:
—This is a guest post by Judith Lee, the Literacy Awards program manager.

The year was 1980, and in Brazil’s teeming metropolis of Rio de Janeiro, Yvonne Bezerra de Mello started Escola Sem Portas Nem Janelas (Schools Without Doors or Windows). The idea was to offer classes on the sidewalk for kids living on the streets.

Things moved along for more than a decade. Then, in 1993, de Mello was devastated when eight of her students were among those killed by militiamen. The incident, known as the Candelária massacre, was a mass shooting by several gunmen directed at homeless teens and children living on the streets.

She dug in, though, and over the ensuing years de Mello developed her sidewalk school into Projeto Uerê, a multi-faceted program that restores learning capacity to children whose cognitive and emotional development have been disrupted by trauma.

This month, the school won the Library of Congress’ top honor in the 2026 Literacy Awards, the $150,000 David M. Rubenstein Prize, bringing the organization resources and international recognition.
snippet: —This is a guest post by Judith Lee, the Literacy Awards program manager.

title: Reid Wiseman: To the Dark Side of the Moon … and Back
content:
Reid Wiseman sat onstage at the National Book Festival, still marveling at the journey that brought him there.

As commander of NASA’s Artemis II mission in April, Wiseman led humanity’s first crewed voyage beyond low Earth orbit in 53 years — a nearly 10-day journey that looped around the moon and back. The deepest moments came on the far side of the moon.

“The moon is blocking our view of Earth. We can’t talk to home,” Wiseman said. “This was an amazing magical period for us, where we were truly alone in the solar system. We were further away than any human had ever been.”

The astounding view — the sun behind the moon, the moon just a black sphere pulling the spacecraft around it — was beyond the power of words to convey. “I don’t think the human mind has evolved to the point of describing what we’re looking at,” he said.

At the furthest point, the crew celebrated with maple cookies, shared a tearful group hug over a crater named for Wiseman’s late wife, Carroll, and heard a posthumous recorded greeting from Apollo 13 commander Jim Lovell: “Welcome to the neighborhood.”

title: The Flowers of Elizabeth Sprague Coolidge, Preserved from Another Century
content:
-This is a guest post by Nyla Adams, an intern in the Office of Communications this summer.

In 1882, a 17-year-old Elizabeth Sprague Coolidge embarked on a grand tour of Europe with her parents, traveling to nearly every country of Western Europe and attending operas whenever possible.

Coolidge kept several journals, including narrative writings and a “botanical diary” of pressed flowers and other greenery representing the places she visited.

Many years after that trip, in 1925, the pianist and composer established the Coolidge Foundation at the Library, providing support for contemporary music to continue through generations, inspiring and shaping the mission of the Library’s Music Division.

Her spectacular album of botanical specimens is a hidden gem preserved in the division’s Elizabeth Sprague Coolidge Foundation Collection, which was fully processed and made available for research last year.

“Alongside her narrative diary and photographs from her European tour, researchers have the opportunity to learn as much about Elizabeth the human as we do about Mrs. Coolidge the benefactor,” said Cait Miller, senior music reference specialist.

title: National Book Festival: Big Crowds and Big Personalities
content:
-NOTE: Our publication schedule was altered last week to accomodate reporting on the death of Dolly Parton. This piece, scheduled for last week, appears now. We knew you’d understand.

The 2026 National Book Festival arrived in style in late August, drawing tens of thousands of bibliophiles, many of whom turned up in festive shirts emblazoned with mottos such as “reading is my favorite sport,” “unreliable narrator,” “sorry, I’m booked” and “bookmarks are for quitters.”

More than 45,000 people attended this year’s event (Aug. 22) at the D.C. convention center, which showcased more than 80 authors and a pavillion full of programs featuring the Library’s collections and resources.

“The promise of a great library is that it opens doors,” said Acting Librarian of Congress Robert R. Newlen, in a short speech that opened the festival. “The Library of Congress has more doors to open than any other library in the world and we hope that you will walk through many of them. Today we have the extraordinary privilege of bringing together some of the most compelling writers and thinkers of our time with all of you, the people who love their work.”
